newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Charges fly between ex-Safrica apartheid agents.
newsitem.headline: Charges fly between ex-Safrica apartheid agents.

text.p: The sinister South Africans who did apartheid's dirty work are turning their fangs on each other, using the murder of Swedish Prime Minister Olof Palme in an increasingly venomous fight.
Three of the apartheid government's most notorious agents have waded into the row over the 1986 assassination in Stockholm, and the first casualty could be the truth.

Eugene de Kock, Dirk Coetzee and Craig Williamson, all assassins and masters of deceit, swapped charges in recent days as the country's Truth and Reconciliation Commission seeks to apportion blame for apartheid atrocities.

De Kock, head of a police hit-squad who has been convicted of six apartheid-era murders, said in court last week that fellow-agent Williamson had carried out the Palme murder as part an operation dubbed "Long Reach".

Williamson, who has acknowledged a role in three bombings of anti-apartheid activists in the 1980s, including the killing of African National Congress member Jeanette Schoon and her daughter, denied the charge.

Coetzee, de Kock's predecessor at the police murder unit, stirred the pot further on Saturday when he said Palme was killed by a former special forces soldier in the then white-run Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe) who was a member of Long Reach.
Williamson, in a telephone interview from Luanda on Sunday, dismissed the charge, which Coetzee admitted was hearsay.
"All I can do is reiterate what I've said before, that I know absolutely nothing about the Palme killing. I haven't been to Sweden since 1978 or 79," Williamson said.

He acknowledged the ex-Rhodesian soldier from the Selous Scouts unit had been in Long Reach, which Williamson described as a company he set up in the late 1980s to conduct political risk analysis for businesses and other clients.
"Long Reach employed former military intelligence agents, and some of them used it as a front for other activities. But it was a genuine political risk consultancy."
Williamson said it appeared Coetzee "just wants to get into the act".
Coetzee defected to the ANC in the late 1980s, the first senior secret police officer to reveal operations by the white minority government against its opponents.
De Kock, who tried to kill Coetzee with a parcel bomb after he defected, described him last week as someone who had gone crawling to the enemy with his hands up.
De Kock said Philip Powell, a senator with the opposition Inkatha Freedom Party, had told him about Williamson's role in killing Palme.
Powell told Reuters on Sunday de Kock was lying: "He seems to be throwing stones in the water and seeing where the ripples reach."
The prosecutor in de Kock's trial took a similar attitude, asking the former police colonel if he also knew the truth about the John F. Kennedy assassination.
All three agents have applied to the truth commission chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu for amnesty for crimes committed in defence of apartheid.

The Afrikaans-language Sunday newspaper Rapport said de Kock's testimony was the start of a "gloves-off" battle between former agents of the secret police. De Kock has accused former presidents P.W. Botha and F.W. de Klerk of knowing about the dirty tricks and said he always acted on orders.
